scenes.narration: Those who met Döme Sztójay at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Born in Versec (modern-day Vršac) into a Serb family as Dimitrije Stojaković (Serbian Cyrillic: Димитрије Стојаковић), Sztójay joined the Austro-Hungarian Army as a young man and served as a colonel during World War I. During the war, he served as an intelligence officer of the general staff of Austria-Hungary.

The private years of Döme Sztójay explain the public decades better than any speech. After the war, Sztójay served in Admiral Miklós Horthy’s counter-revolutionary Royal Hungarian Army, specializing in counter-espionage. Regarded as an expert in military intelligence, Sztójay founded the military intelligence service of the Honved (Royal Hungarian Army) and served as the first director of the intelligence service.

The family Döme Sztójay came from matters more than the legends admit. As someone who specialised in the murky business of espionage and moreover had a well deserved reputation as an intriguer, Sztójay was widely regarded as a ruthless schemer who was always engaged in plots to advance his interests. After Horthy became Regent of Hungary, Sztójay was promoted to general and served as a military attaché in Berlin from 1927 to 1933.

The first real success of Döme Sztójay arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. During his time in Berlin, Sztójay formed close links with the elite of the Reichswehr officers and came to have a profound admiration for the Prussian-German militarism. In 1932, he signed a secret agreement that called for German-Hungarian co-operation in intelligence operations, especially against Czechoslovakia.

The last chapter of Döme Sztójay was written long after the fame. In 1935, Prime Minister Gyula Gömbös named Sztójay as Hungarian ambassador to Germany, a position he would hold until 1944. As ambassador, Sztójay formed strong ties with the Third Reich and often voiced support for German policies to his superiors in Hungary.

The whole life of Döme Sztójay reads like a single decision repeated. Sztójay regarded himself as representing the Hungarian General Staff instead of the Foreign Ministry in Berlin. He viewed a German-Hungarian alliance as natural as Germany rejected the Treaty of Versailles while Hungary rejected the Treaty of Trianon.

Between the birth and the legend of Döme Sztójay lie the years that actually decide it. France had signed treaties of alliances with Czechoslovakia in 1924, Romania in 1926, and Yugoslavia in 1927. Since Germany's enemy was also France, Sztójay believed that a German-Hungarian alliance was essential for both nations, and he worked hard to achieve that goal.

The reputation of Döme Sztójay was built in the middle, not at the edges. Sztójay felt that his nominal superior, the Foreign Minister Kálmán Kánya, was not doing enough to advance a German-Hungarian alliance, and he set about undermining Kánya's authority. During 1937 and 1938, Sztójay acted in a highly subordinate manner as he worked to achieve an alliance with the Reich while intriguing against Kánya.

Somebody like Döme Sztójay should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Acting on his own, Sztójay in January 1937 approached the German War Minister, General Werner von Blomberg, to ask for staff talks between the German General Staff and the Hungarian General Staff for a joint plan of war against Czechoslovakia. During the time that Count Pál Teleki was prime minister for a second time from 1939 to 1941, Sztójay worked closely with the Defense Minister Károly Bartha, and the chief of the general staff, General Henrik Werth, in seeking to undermine Teleki's foreign policy.

The life of Döme Sztójay begins far from where the story usually starts. Sztójay often leaked information to the Germans and made it clear he did not support Teleki. Sztójay later boasted that the soldiers of the Honved were "a major indeed decisive, factor in the development of the German-Hungarian relationship" with the clear implication that it was the Honved rather than the civilian leaders who were responsible for the German-Hungarian alliance.

Döme Sztójay was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In late 1939, Sztójay was joined in his plots by Colonel Sándor Homlok who arrived in Berlin in late 1939 as the military attaché. Homlok had devised a plan in September 1938 for aircraft bearing the colors of the Czechoslovak Air Force to bomb a city in Hungary in order to provide a casus belli for Hungary to invade Czechoslovakia.

To understand where Döme Sztójay ended up, start with where Döme Sztójay began. In late March 1941 during a visit to the Reich Chancellery to meet Adolf Hitler, Sztójay became probably the first Hungarian to learn of Operation Barbarossa. Hitler told Sztójay that he had "lost patience" with the Soviet Union and he was planning to take drastic action, which Sztójay correctly guessed meant that Germany was going to invade the Soviet Union in the very near-future.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Döme Sztójay ran through years nobody filmed. The matter was considered important enough that Hitler lent Sztójay an airplane to take him to Budapest to personally deliver the letter to the regent. Teleki  stayed up late, trying to talk Horthy out of accepting Hitler's offer.

Each stage of the life of Döme Sztójay made the next stage possible. Teleki's two arguments were the likely British reaction to Hungary attacking Yugoslavia and the problem of calling reservists serving as farmers at time of widespread flooding in the countryside. For the letter to take back to Berlin, Teleki drafted an ambiguous reply, saying that Hungary accepted the offer, but only assist Germany "in accordance with its power", which for Teleki meant rejection as Hungary had difficult relations with Romania and concentrated troops along the border.

The people who knew Döme Sztójay young describe someone already restless. However, Sztójay when he returned to Berlin told Hitler that the letter meant Hungarian acceptance of his offer. On 4 April 1941, when Bartha visited Berlin to see Hitler Sztójay accompanied him to the Reich Chancellery.

What Döme Sztójay built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. During the meeting with Hitler, both Bartha and Sztójay put forward a plan for a false flag attack to have Hungary join the invasion of Yugoslavia. The plan called for German aircraft to be painted with the colors of the Royal Yugoslav Air Force to bomb a city in southern Hungary with Szeged being given as the best target in order to bring Hungary into the war.

By the time Döme Sztójay reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. On 6 April 1941, when Germany invaded Yugoslavia, Szeged was bombed by aircraft described as Yugoslav. Sakmyster accused Sztójay and Homlok of being the men who organised the bombing of Kassa in June 1941, perhaps with the support and approval of Werth.

The rise of Döme Sztójay was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Starting in May 1941, Sztójay sent regular reports to Budapest predicating that the Germany was going to invade the Soviet Union and demanded that Hungary take part. When Operation Barbarossa was launched on 22 June 1941, Sztójay immediately started to demand that Hungary take part in "the crusade against Bolshevism" as Hitler called the war, and was intensely disappointed when prime minister László Bárdossy did not heed his advice.

Setbacks came early for Döme Sztójay, and the response to them is the real story. Sakmyster argued that Sztójay and Homlok would have not had approached Hitler, who left Berlin for his Wolfsschanze (Wolf's Lair) headquarters deep in the forests of East Prussia right after Operation Barbarossa was launched, where he stayed for most of the summer of 1941. Instead, Sakmyster argued that Sztójay who was friends with numerous Wehrmacht generals would had gone to the Wehrmacht for help with the bombing, knowing that the Wehrmacht generals were more open to having the Honved join Barbarossa than Hitler was.

The legacy of Döme Sztójay outlived the circumstances that produced it. Sakmyster maintained that the conspirators engaged in a false flag operation of this sort would not had written anything done since an operation of this sort would had been treason. In Operation Margarethe in March 1944, the German Army occupied Hungary and forced Horthy to remove Prime Minister Miklós Kállay from office.

Few lives travel as far as that of Döme Sztójay, and the distance is the point. Kállay, like Horthy, knew that Germany was losing the war, and had put out numerous feelers to the West. On 9 September 1943 László Veress, an employee of the Ministry of Exterior signed a secret agreement to surrender unconditionally to the Western Allies.

The childhood of Döme Sztójay contains the adult in small print. Although Kállay and his government had promised on numerous occasions to surrender to the Western Allies as soon as they reached Hungary, Veress' agreement was unauthorized, as in Kállay's consideration it effectively gave up Hungary's sovereignty. When they took over the country, the Germans gave Horthy a choice between choosing a new prime minister who would cooperate with the Germans or undisguised occupation.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Döme Sztójay — in that order. Knowing that the latter would likely mean a Gauleiter who would treat Hungary in the same manner as the other Nazi-occupied countries, Horthy chose the former. The German Plenipotentiary for Hungary, Edmund Veesenmayer, proposed that Horthy reappoint Béla Imrédy, who had been prime minister earlier in the war (and who had, ironically, a Jewish great-grandfather).

The turning point in the life of Döme Sztójay looked like a failure at the time. However, Horthy balked at appointing the strongly pro-German Imrédy and suggested Sztójay instead. Though Sztójay had been ambassador to Berlin for a decade and was known to be pro-German, Horthy believed that at bottom he was a soldier first and would not totally give in to German demands.

Every biography of Döme Sztójay has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. The Germans readily approved of Horthy's choice, and on 23 March 1944, Sztójay was appointed prime minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs. Shortly after being appointed prime minister, Sztójay met SS-Obergruppenführer Ernst Kaltenbrunner, who had arrived in Budapest with the German invasion.

The education of Döme Sztójay happened mostly outside any school. The transcript of the Sztójay-Kaltenbrunner meeting was destroyed afterwards, but accordingly to Imrédy who also attended the meeting, an agreement was reached for the extermination of all entire Hungarian Jewish community. On 13 April and again on 23 April 1944, Cardinal Serédi met Sztójay to complain about the way his government treated Jewish converts to Catholicism, but Sztójay told him that he should focus on praying for a victory over "Bolshevism" instead.

What Döme Sztójay wanted at the start and what Döme Sztójay got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Despite requests from several bishops, Cardinal Serédi never publicly condemned the genocide that Sztójay was perpetuating against Hungarian Jews out the grounds that Sztójay might persecute Catholics and that the best course was to stay silent. As prime minister, Sztójay legalized Ferenc Szálasi's Arrow Cross Party, increased Hungarian troop levels on the Eastern Front, dissolved the nation's labor unions, jailed political opponents, and cracked down on left wing politicians and activists.

The defining trait of Döme Sztójay was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Horthy became appalled by Sztójay's actions and demanded his removal as prime minister, but Veesenmayer, backed by Adolf Hitler, sternly refused to do so. In early June 1944, Horthy first wrote to Sztójay about the "Jewish Question", saying that he had just heard disturbing reports of inhumane treatment of Hungarian Jews.

Those who met Döme Sztójay at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Horthy asked  Sztójay to exempt from the racial laws Jewish converts to Christianity along with Jewish doctors, engineers and businessmen. Horthy noted a disproportionate number of businessmen, doctors and engineers in Hungary were Jewish and that Sztójay's anti-Semitic campaign had pushed the economy to the brink of collapse as while making it almost impossible for many people to receive medical treatment.

The private years of Döme Sztójay explain the public decades better than any speech. Horthy's letter to Sztójay in early June 1944 was the first time that he mentioned the deportations as he himself noted that he just heard these reports. Horthy and his family claimed that he did not know about the Holocaust until early July 1944 and that the reason why he took no action in May-June 1944 was because he did not know that all the Jews being deported would be exterminated.

The family Döme Sztójay came from matters more than the legends admit. Horthy's daughter-in-law, Ilona Horthy, stated the regent first learned about the Holocaust on 3 July 1944 and that until then he had no idea what was happening to his Jewish subjects. On 29 June 1944, Cardinal Serédi, under pressure from his bishops, wrote a pastoral letter that criticised the deportations of the Jews as against divine law and demanded the deportations stop immediately.
